description: We’re Team NBE, three nutrition undergraduates from Brazil (one also holds a Physical Education degree and studies software development). For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we built a platform where astronauts log meals, fluids, exercise, sleep and mood in under two minutes, turning them into risk signals based on NASA standards and structured data for researchers on Earth. A Ground Control view and a food stores forecast help professionals plan better nutrition for long-duration missions.
summary:
NBE (Nutrition Beyond Earth) is a health monitoring platform that helps astronauts on long missions see, understand and act on their own health, starting from the one indicator they control every day: what they eat. In a check-in of less than two minutes, each crew member logs meals, fluids, exercise, sleep, mood, fatigue and a body check (resting heart rate and symptoms).
NBE compares this data with NASA standards (NASA-STD-3001 and JSC-67378) and turns it into a Crew Readiness Score and six risk signals tied to the hazards named in the challenge: bone, body mass, hydration, mind, immune and heart. Every signal comes with an action the astronaut can take on board, without waiting for Earth.
At the same time, every entry becomes structured data for researchers and flight surgeons on the ground, tagged with space weather from NASA's DONKI API. NBE's rules were checked against real NASA flight results from the ISS. Because 200 days from home, staying healthy can't wait for an answer from Houston.
details:
Would you notice your body falling behind... 200 days from Earth?

On the way to Mars there is no doctor's office down the hall. There are months in transit, minutes of delay on every message and no possible evacuation. Astronauts become their own first line of defense, and the first signs of trouble are often on the plate.

The problem hidden in every meal

NASA's own data shows it. In 25 ISS crew members, intake stayed at about 80% of the energy they needed and body weight fell by 2.8% to 4.4%, almost all of it in the first month (Zwart et al., 2014). Without full protection, crews lost 1% to 2% of bone density per month (Spector et al., NASA).

The good news: nutrition is a countermeasure that works. In 42 astronauts, those who trained on the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED) and kept energy and vitamin D adequate came back with bone density practically the same as before flight (Smith et al., NASA). Today this monitoring depends on Earth. On the way to Mars, it can't.

What NBE is

NBE is a personal health dashboard for each crew member and a control panel for the ground team. It gathers daily indicators, evaluates them against NASA standards and tells the astronaut what to do next, on board and right away. All rules are transparent: every number has a source and every alert shows why.

Features

1. Launch screen and demo notice

The opening screen introduces NBE and makes it clear from the start that this is a prototype: a test build made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, with sample data, and not a medical device or an official NASA product. Flight mode uses dark colors and almost no animation, to avoid eye strain in a confined environment.

Screenshot 1 — Launch screen with the DEMO notice.

2. Crew profiles with PIN

Up to six crew members, each with a seat and a 3-digit PIN (in the demo, 111 to 666). The PIN is checked automatically on the last digit, with no unlock button. The Readiness Score is only shown to the person signed in to their own profile, so it does not create competition between crewmates.

The seventh profile is Ground Control, the ground team's view, which sees the whole crew. In the prototype the PIN is only a privacy screen, not real security.

Screenshot 2 — Choosing a profile (Crew roster).

Screenshot 3 — PIN keypad.

3. Dashboard: Crew Readiness Score

A number from 0 to 100 that answers the question at the top of the screen: "Is your body keeping up with the mission?". It is the weighted average of eight components: energy balance, protein, bone nutrients (calcium and vitamin D), hydration, exercise adherence, sleep, mood and appetite, and perceived fatigue.

The "Why this score" panel shows each component, how much it is worth and how many points it gained or lost compared with the previous day. The 7-day chart marks the OK, Watch and Act bands, because one bad day is not a trend.

Screenshot 4 — Readiness Score, score breakdown and 7-day trend.

4. Risk Radar

Six signals tied to the hazards named in the challenge, sorted from most to least urgent. Each one has three states (OK, Watch and Act) and shows the reason in one line. They are risk signals, never a diagnosis.

Screenshot 5 — Risk Radar with the six signals.

5. NASA flight reference

Next to the crew member's data, NBE shows what happened to real ISS crews: 1% to 2% bone loss per month, 2% to 5% loss of body mass in the first month and 80 to 160 mSv of radiation every six months. All of this is converted to the current mission day (on Day 42, for example, 1.4% to 2.8% of bone and 18 to 37 mSv).

The radiation block also notes when NASA's DONKI API recorded a solar event in the past week. It is context, not a prediction: the on-board dosimeter remains the real measurement.

Screenshot 6 — NASA flight reference: bone, body mass and radiation.

6. Two-minute check-in: meals

The on-board menu follows NASA's Artemis II crew menu. All 38 items have sourced nutrients per serving: 37 from USDA FoodData Central and 1 from TACO, the Brazilian Food Composition Table (pão de queijo, Brazilian cheese bread). Each card shows the serving, calories, protein and calcium, and how many units are still on board.

To keep it fast: favorites, filters by food group and a "Same as yesterday" button that copies the previous day's meals. The timer at the bottom shows check-in time against the 2-minute goal, along with the day's totals.

Screenshot 7 — Meals from the Artemis II menu, with serving, nutrients and stock.

7. Fluids and vitamin D

+250 ml and +500 ml buttons log fluids in one tap. The target is 32 ml per kg of body weight per day, with a minimum of 2,500 ml for men and 2,100 ml for women (NASA JSC-67378). A toggle records the daily vitamin D supplement (800 IU, the dose used by ISS astronauts since 2006, per Smith et al., 2012).

Screenshot 8 — Fluids and vitamin D.

8. Exercise

The target follows the ISS routine: 90 minutes of resistance training (ARED) and 60 minutes of aerobic exercise, 6 days a week, with one scheduled rest day (Loehr et al., NASA). Adherence goes from 0% to 100% and stops at the cap, so training beyond the plan does not inflate the score. Each hour of extravehicular activity (EVA) adds 200 kcal to the day's target (NASA-STD-3001).

Screenshot 9 — Exercise following NASA's ISS routine.

9. Sleep, mood and fatigue

Hours of sleep, mood on five levels and perceived fatigue on the Samn-Perelli scale used by NASA Ames' fatigue laboratory (from 1, fully alert, to 7, exhausted). Fatigue of 5 or more raises an alert on the Mind signal. The sleep target is 8 h, within the 8.5 h NASA schedules for sleep on the ISS. Since astronauts slept 6.1 h on average (Barger et al., 2014), less than 6 h also raises an alert.

Screenshot 10 — Sleep, mood and fatigue (Samn-Perelli scale).

10. Appetite and menu fatigue

Normal appetite counts as 100%. Eating less or more than usual takes points away linearly, in both directions. The "Menu fatigue" toggle records when the crew member is tired of the menu options, a known problem on long missions.

Screenshot 11 — Appetite and menu fatigue.

11. Body check

Morning resting heart rate (optional), today's symptoms linked to the immune changes NASA observes in flight (skin rash, stuffy nose or sore throat, cold sores, fever, upset stomach) and cardiac warning signs. A warning sign, such as chest pain, immediately shows a prompt to contact the flight surgeon.

Screenshot 12 — Body check: resting heart rate, symptoms and warning signs.

12. Act Now

Every signal in Watch or Act becomes a concrete on-board task with a Done button. Examples: opening an item from the bonus container for menu fatigue, or swapping an item that is running low for another from the same food group with similar nutrients. NASA already plans to move more medical decisions from the ground to the spacecraft, and NBE was built for that model.

Screenshot 13 — Act Now: today's actions.

13. Ground Link

Houston reviews the records and sends messages that arrive with a simulated communication delay, such as item swap suggestions or target adjustments. The crew member accepts or declines them on board.

Every day becomes a structured record (no names, only the crew code), with a documented schema and CSV and JSON export, ready for researchers and flight surgeons. Each record carries space weather context from NASA's DONKI API.

Screenshot 14 — Message from Houston with swap suggestions.

Screenshot 15 — Daily records with CSV and JSON export.

14. Ground Control

The ground team's view shows the whole crew in one place: who has checked in, how many are in Act or Watch, each member's signals and the day's nutrients. It also shows the food stores summary and lets the team reset crew PINs.

Screenshot 16 — Ground Control: crew overview.

15. Food stores

A single ship-wide inventory, fed by the check-in itself: stock = last count + resupplies + adjustments − logged servings. The chart shows the energy on board in days of crew need and the projection to the end of the mission.

The table shows, for each item, daily use, days of supply, when it runs out and the rationing that would make it last until the end of the mission plus a 14-day margin. Resupply mass is estimated at 2.36 kg of packaged food per crew member per day (Lynch & Goodliff, NASA, 2023).

Screenshot 17 — Energy on board and projection to the end of the mission.

Screenshot 18 — Items on board: days of supply, run-out dates and status.

16. Checked against NASA flight data

NBE's rules were tested against real ISS results. At 80% of the energy needed, as observed in 25 crew members, the Body Mass signal goes to Act within the first week, before most of the weight loss happens. For bone, the signal is only OK when resistance training, calcium, protein and vitamin D are all on track: the same factors that separated astronauts who kept their bone from those who lost it.

Screenshot 19 — What NASA observed on the ISS and what NBE would do.

17. Test mode: skip days

A "Test" bar on the Dashboard, in the Ground Control view and in About has "Skip a day" and "Skip 7 days" buttons. They move the mission day forward for the whole crew, so judges can test NBE over several days. Check-ins stay on the days they were made, the food stores keep going down by what was logged and the counter stops at the last day of the mission. "Reset demo data" goes back to Day 42.

Tools and technologies used

  • Languages: a single HTML file, with the CSS (visuals) and JavaScript (logic and calculations) written inside it, with no server; the data stays in the browser.
  • Charts: SVG drawn in code; Three.js for the opening animation.
  • Data: NASA's DONKI API, NASA standards and technical reports, USDA FoodData Central and TACO.
  • Design: Figma; Public Sans and DM Mono typefaces from the NASA Web Design System, and Archivo for headings.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

NBE's health logic does not use AI to make decisions. The Readiness Score and every signal follow transparent rules, built from NASA standards and stored in a configuration file with the source of each number, so every result can be traced and audited. AI tools supported the team's work:

  • Claude (Anthropic): assisted with programming the app's backend; automated tests of the screens and calculations.
  • ChatGPT (OpenAI, GPT-6 Astra): helping translate and review the texts.
  • Figma: design of the screens and the visual identity.
  • ElevenLabs: the narration of the demo video was generated by AI (synthetic voice), from a script written by us.

How NBE works

The astronaut acts on board right away; Earth learns from every record and adjusts the targets over time.

On board, the check-in becomes a score, signals and actions on the same day. On Earth, the records reach Ground Control, which sends back adjusted targets when communication allows.

Why it matters on Earth

The same engine works wherever a small group eats from a fixed supply, far from help.

Our mission: fuel for the long way home

The next giant leap will be taken by people, and people run on food. NBE turns every meal into a health signal, every signal into an action and every action into data that makes the next mission safer. NBE supports, not replaces, the flight surgeon.
